title: Impact of cataract surgery on subjective fall risk and mobility
summary:
The operation, in which a clouded eye lens is replaced with an artificial lens, is one of the most common procedures worldwide. In addition to improving vision, it could also help people walk more safely, maintain better balance, and fall less often. However, previous studies have come to different conclusions: some found no clear link to fewer falls, while more recent evaluations suggest improvements in mobility and balance. What has often been neglected so far is the subjective feeling of safety—in other words, whether those affected actually feel safer in everyday life.

The aim of this study is therefore to investigate whether the operation improves general mobility and the personal feeling of being at risk of falling. It will also examine whether certain groups benefit differently – for example, depending on age, number of other diseases, or type of artificial lens used.

interventions.name: Included are consecutive patients ≥ 60 years of age with planned cataract surgery at the study center who are capable of giving informed consent and who can answer the questionnaires independently or with assistance.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Indication/planning of cataract surgery
Capacity to give consent, sufficient understanding to participate Willingness to participate in pre- and post-operative interviews (follow-up approx. 3 months)
Exclusion criteria:
Acute neurological illness (e.g., stroke within the last 3 months)
Severe cognitive impairment (e.g., severe dementia)
Relevant ophthalmological comorbidities with a significant impact on visual function (e.g., advanced age-related macular degeneration, optic atrophy)
Planned major orthopedic surgery within the next 3 months
Serious postoperative ocular complication that prevents valid follow-up
